# Gelatox

> A single-page buyer's guide to Gelatox, a skin, hair and nail gummy supplement sold as 60 gummies per bottle and taken two gummies daily. Written for readers in the United States at https://gelatox-us.vercel.app/. Orders complete on the official checkout. Last reviewed 17 November 2026.

Gelatox is a chewable vitamin supplement aimed at skin vitality, hair strength and nail condition. The maker describes it as a 100% natural formula that speeds cell renewal, strengthens the skin's protective barrier for hydration, and supplies antioxidants against free radicals. The serving is two gummies daily, taken about 30 minutes before a morning or afternoon meal with a full glass of water, so one 60-gummy bottle lasts 30 days. The official listing names six nutrients — biotin, vitamin B12 as methylcobalamin, vitamin B6 as pyridoxine hydrochloride, folate, pantothenic acid as d-calcium pantothenate, and vitamin A — but publishes no milligram, microgram or Daily Value figure for any of them, no other ingredients and no allergen statement; the Supplement Facts panel appears online only as an image. Three packages are sold: two bottles at $79 each ($158 plus an unstated shipping charge, about $2.63 a day before postage), three bottles at $69 each ($207 with free US shipping, about $2.30 a day) and six bottles at $49 each ($294 with free US shipping, about $1.63 a day). Six digital bonus guides, valued by the seller at $358 in total, come with the three and six bottle packages. Every package carries a 60-day Results or Refund Guarantee. One payment, no subscription. Sold to adults 18 and over.

## Sources cited on this page

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: biotin](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/biotin-consumer/): states there is little scientific evidence that biotin supplements improve hair, skin or nails, and warns that high intakes can cause false results in some laboratory tests including thyroid hormone testing.
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: vitamin A](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminA-Consumer/): recommended intakes and upper limits for vitamin A, relevant because no amount is published for this product.
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: what you need to know](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WYNTK-Consumer/): a plain-language primer on what dietary supplements are and how they are regulated.
- [MedlinePlus: skin, hair and nails](https://medlineplus.gov/skinhairandnails.html): consumer background on hair loss, nail disease and skin conditions, and when to seek a diagnosis.
- [NIH News in Health: keep your skin healthy](https://newsinhealth.nih.gov/2015/11/keep-your-skin-healthy): washing, moisturising and sun-protection basics from the National Institutes of Health.
- [FDA: dietary supplements](https://www.fda.gov/food/dietary-supplements): supplements fall under food law rather than medicines law in the United States, with no pre-market approval.
- [FTC: health claims](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing/health-claims): the advertising rules a supplement health claim has to meet.
